symptoms: joint pain that worsens with movement
guidance: Maintain a healthy weight (reduces joint load). Low‑impact exercises (walking, swimming, cycling) improve function. Use assistive devices (cane, walker). For pain: paracetamol, topical NSAIDs; avoid long‑term oral NSAIDs (GI/renal risk). If severe, joint replacement is available free under PMJAY. Physiotherapy is essential.
precautions: Avoid high‑impact activities (jumping, running)
Use walking aids if needed
Do not exceed recommended doses of painkillers
If you have kidney disease, avoid NSAIDs
Attend physiotherapy sessions regularly

symptoms: sudden severe pain in the hip or back after a fall or minor trauma
shortening or rotation of the leg (hip fracture)
may occur without obvious trauma (fragility fracture)
guidance: Any fall or sudden back pain in an elderly person should raise suspicion of a fracture. Seek emergency care immediately. Hip fracture requires surgical fixation; vertebral fracture may be managed conservatively or with vertebroplasty. Prevention: calcium (1200 mg/day), vitamin D (800 IU/day), bisphosphonates, and fall prevention strategies.
precautions: Remove fall hazards at home (rugs, clutter)
Install grab bars in bathrooms
Ensure adequate lighting
If you have osteoporosis, take prescribed medications
Get a DEXA scan to assess bone density

symptoms: progressive loss of muscle mass and strength
difficulty climbing stairs, rising from a chair
guidance: Protein intake is crucial – aim for 1.2–1.5 g/kg body weight per day (egg, fish, poultry, dairy, legumes). Resistance exercises (light weights, elastic bands) at least 2‑3 times weekly. Vitamin D and calcium supplementation. If severe, consider oral nutritional supplements. Early intervention prevents disability.
precautions: Eat protein‑rich foods at every meal
Engage in strength training exercises
Maintain adequate hydration
Monitor weight monthly
If you have poor appetite, see a nutritionist

guidance: Frailty is a state of vulnerability. Comprehensive geriatric assessment is needed. Interventions: nutritional support (high‑protein, high‑calorie), progressive resistance training, fall prevention, medication review (polypharmacy), and social support. Early detection helps prevent disability.

If you feel weak, speak to your doctor

Review all medications (some can cause weakness)

symptoms: acute onset of confusion (hours to days)
often precipitated by infection, dehydration, or medication
guidance: Delirium is a medical emergency – seek care immediately. Identify and treat the underlying cause (UTI, pneumonia, electrolyte imbalance, drug effect). Environmental measures: reorient patient, provide familiar objects, calm environment. Avoid restraints. Family presence helps. Use low‑dose antipsychotics only if agitation is severe.
precautions: If a loved one suddenly becomes confused, seek emergency care
Do not assume it is dementia – delirium is reversible
Keep the environment calm and familiar
Ensure adequate hydration and nutrition
Review all medications for offending drugs

symptoms: history of hypertension, diabetes, or stroke
guidance: Management: control vascular risk factors (blood pressure, lipids, diabetes). Antiplatelet therapy (aspirin) if indicated. Cognitive rehabilitation and supportive care. Prevention: lifestyle (diet, exercise, smoking cessation). Free medications at NCD clinics.
precautions: Strictly control BP, blood sugar, and cholesterol
Take antiplatelet medications as prescribed
Maintain a healthy diet and exercise
If you have a stroke, get immediate care

symptoms: REM sleep behaviour disorder (acting out dreams)
guidance: Cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil) may help hallucinations. Avoid antipsychotics (severe sensitivity). Manage Parkinsonism with levodopa cautiously (may worsen psychosis). Non‑pharmacological: routine, safety measures, caregiver support. Specialist referral is essential.

Use cholinesterase inhibitors as prescribed
Fall prevention is crucial (gait impairment)
If you have hallucinations, do not argue – redirect

symptoms: personality and behaviour changes (apathy, disinhibition, loss of empathy)
relatively preserved memory in early stages
guidance: Behavioural management is key: structured routines, caregiver education. Speech therapy for language. Medications for agitation (antipsychotics used cautiously). Genetic counselling if familial. Free care at government psychiatry/neurology departments.

If you have changes in personality, see a neurologist
Caregiver support is crucial

symptoms: preserved functional abilities (independent in daily activities)
increased risk of progression to Alzheimer's
guidance: MCI is a transitional state. Management: cognitive stimulation (games, reading), physical exercise, social engagement. Control vascular risk factors. Medications are not routinely recommended. Regular follow‑up to monitor progression. Free cognitive screening at government hospitals.
precautions: Engage in mentally stimulating activities
Maintain a healthy lifestyle
If you have memory concerns, see a doctor
Manage blood pressure and diabetes

symptoms: increased risk of adverse drug reactions
often associated with multiple chronic conditions
guidance: Regular medication review by a geriatrician or pharmacist is essential. Use the STOPP/START criteria to deprescribe inappropriate medications. Simplify dosing schedules. Use non‑drug alternatives where possible. Always bring all medications (including OTC) to each doctor visit.

Keep an updated medication list
Ask your doctor if any medication can be reduced or stopped
Avoid OTC drugs without consulting

symptoms: suicidal ideation (higher risk in elderly men)
guidance: Depression is not a normal part of ageing. Treatment: SSRIs (sertraline, escitalopram) are first‑line – avoid TCAs (anticholinergic). Psychotherapy (CBT) and social support are effective. Screen annually. If suicidal, seek emergency care. Free mental health services at DMHP centers.
precautions: If you feel persistently sad, talk to a doctor
Engage in social activities
Do not self‑medicate with alcohol
If you have thoughts of harming yourself, call helpline

symptoms: fear of falling or health catastrophizing
guidance: Anxiety is common and treatable. CBT, relaxation techniques, and SSRIs (sertraline). Avoid benzodiazepines (risk of falls and cognitive impairment). Free counseling at government hospitals. Address underlying causes (pain, social isolation).
precautions: Avoid benzodiazepines – they increase fall risk
Practice deep breathing
Stay connected with loved ones

symptoms: preoccupation with having a serious illness
normal bodily sensations are interpreted as disease signs
guidance: CBT is effective. Set a regular follow‑up schedule with a trusted physician (avoid excessive testing). Address anxiety and depression. Avoid over‑investigation. Free counselling available.

Stick to one primary care doctor
Do not demand unnecessary tests
If you have health anxiety, seek therapy
Limit checking behaviour (e.g., pulse, BP)

guidance: Combat loneliness: community groups, senior citizen clubs, telephone check‑ins, and volunteer work. Technology training for video calls. Family involvement is crucial. Government programs have community outreach. Mental health support if needed.

Join a local senior group
Use technology to connect
If you have no one to talk to, call a helpline

symptoms: caregiver preventing access to the elder
guidance: Elder abuse is a crime. Report to local police or helpline (1091, 181, or senior helplines). Ensure safety – move to a safe place if needed. Medical care for injuries. Legal aid and shelter options are available. Raise awareness.

Do not confront the abuser alone
If you are being abused, talk to a trusted person
Keep important documents and phone numbers handy
Know the local helpline numbers

guidance: Comprehensive fall risk assessment: vision, hearing, muscle strength, balance, and home safety. If you have a fall, get medical evaluation.

guidance: Prevent: rise slowly, sit on the edge of the bed for 1‑2 minutes before standing. Avoid dehydration – drink adequate fluids. If medication‑induced, adjust dose (under doctor's supervision). Wear compression stockings. If falls occur, get reviewed.

guidance: Pelvic floor exercises (Kegel) are effective for both sexes. Bladder training: timed voiding, double voiding. Medications: anticholinergics (oxybutynin) or mirabegron – avoid if contraindicated. If severe, urological evaluation. Avoid caffeine and alcohol. Incontinence is not normal – seek help.

Limit caffeine and alcohol

symptoms: often due to muscle weakness, nerve damage, or chronic constipation (overflow)
guidance: Rule out constipation (impaction). Use fibre and fluids to achieve soft, formed stool. Pelvic floor physiotherapy. Medications: loperamide for urgency. If persistent, gastroenterology referral. Protect skin with barrier creams. Free physiotherapy at government hospitals.

Stay hydrated
Do not ignore – it is treatable

Use protective underwear if needed

guidance: Increase dietary fibre (fruits, vegetables, whole grains) and fluids (unless fluid‑restricted). Regular exercise. Increase fibre gradually to avoid bloating

symptoms: trouble understanding speech in noisy places
guidance: Get a hearing assessment – free at government ENT clinics. Hearing aids improve quality of life and reduce cognitive decline. Communication strategies: face the speaker, reduce background noise, speak slowly. Avoid loud noise. If sudden hearing loss, seek emergency (steroids).

If you have hearing loss, get hearing aids
When speaking, ask people to face you

guidance: Glaucoma is a leading cause of irreversible blindness. Screening: annual eye exam for those >40, especially with family history. guidance: Sip water frequently, suck on sugar‑free lozenges. Use artificial saliva or mouthwashes for dryness. Avoid caffeine, alcohol, and tobacco. Good oral hygiene is essential. If medication‑induced, discuss alternatives. Regular dental checkups.

guidance: Common with ageing. Provide flavourful, well‑seasoned foods (use herbs and spices). Ensure safety: check gas appliances regularly, label foods with dates. Consider zinc supplements if deficient. If sudden loss, rule out infection or neurological cause.
